templates.title: Collaborative playlists: who adds, and whose additions others remove
templates.subtopic: LEAD per (playlist, track), pairing an event with the next one, deduplication

sections.scenario: A music app lets a playlist's owner invite friends to edit it together: anyone in a collaborative playlist can add tracks and remove them. The product team wants to know how collaboration goes in practice: how many tracks each collaborator adds to each playlist, and how often an addition is taken out again quickly by someone else, a sign of disagreement about what belongs on the playlist.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns playlist_id, user_id, additions, removed_by_others, removed_share: one row per playlist and user with at least one addition, ordered by playlist_id, user_id. additions counts the user's add events in the playlist. An addition's removal is the next event for the same playlist and track, in event_ts, event_id order, if that event is a remove. removed_by_others counts the user's additions whose removal was made by a different user within 24 hours of the addition (at most 24 hours after it). removed_share = removed_by_others / additions, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{scope_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Exactly 24 hours counts as within 24 hours; 24 hours and one second does not. A removal by the user who added the track never counts. The sample has {{playlists}} playlists and {{events}} event rows.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical playlists, users and events. Timestamps are UTC. The event log is the only source: there is no table of the playlist's current contents.
sections.criteria: Pairs each addition with the next event for its playlist and track, in a deterministic order; counts only removals by someone else; inclusive 24-hour bound; collaborative playlists only (Hard+); duplicates collapsed before LEAD (Very Hard); correct counts, rounding and order; can discuss offline edits, small-sample ranking and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: Who counts as a collaborator?
clarifications.a: Anyone with at least one addition in the playlist; the owner included.

clarifications.q: A track is added, removed by its adder, and added again by someone else. Which removal belongs to which addition?
clarifications.a: Each addition is paired with the next event for that playlist and track only. The first addition's removal is the self-removal; a later removal belongs to the re-add.

clarifications.q: Is a removal exactly 24 hours later within 24 hours?
clarifications.a: Yes. At most 24 hours after the addition counts.

clarifications.q: Two events for the same track have the same timestamp.
clarifications.a: event_id breaks the tie.

clarifications.q: How is the share rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of removed_by_others over additions, half away from zero.

hints: LEAD(action), LEAD(user_id) and LEAD(event_ts) over PARTITION BY playlist_id, track_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id give each addition the event that follows it.
Keep only add rows after the window function, not before it: filtering first throws away the removals you are looking for.
If rows can repeat, remove the copies before LEAD; a doubled addition would otherwise become its own "next event".
followups: The product team also wants "additions still on the playlist today". How would you get that from the same log, and what changes if the log has gaps?
Collaborators edit offline, and their edits arrive hours later with device timestamps. What does that do to "within 24 hours" and to the pairing of add and remove?
Rank playlists by how contentious they are. Why is removed_share alone a poor ranking for playlists with three additions, and what would you use instead?
At hundreds of millions of playlist events a day, how would you compute this daily without rescanning history, when a removal can arrive up to 24 hours after the addition it closes?

rules.ask: A track was removed and added back twice. Which removals does your join attach to the first addition, and should it?
If you filter to additions before the window function, what does LEAD return?
A retried addition is logged twice. Without deduplication, what is the first copy's next event, and how does that change removed_by_others?
Is your comparison inclusive at exactly 24 hours, and what would a 23-hour day do if you compared calendar times instead?
Does the owner removing a friend's addition count, and does your query treat the owner differently from anyone else?

templates.title: Release-day share of first-week streams, at each market's local midnight
templates.subtopic: time zones with AT TIME ZONE, local calendar days, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A streaming service releases a new album at midnight local time in each market, so the release rolls around the world over a day. The label team asks, for each album and market, how front-loaded the first week was: the share of first-week streams that happened on release day itself. Streams are logged as UTC instants; each market has one time zone for releases.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns album_id, market, first_week_streams, release_day_streams, release_day_share, ordered by album_id, market. A stream's local date is its stream_ts in the market's time zone (markets.tz). Its day number is its local date minus the album's release_date. Release day is day 0, and the first week is days 0 to 6. first_week_streams counts the pair's streams in the first week, release_day_streams those on day 0, and release_day_share is their ratio rounded to 4 decimal places. {{week_rule}} {{min_rule}} {{dst_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Each row in streams is one stream: this exercise's counting rule has already been applied. The sample has {{streams}} streams in {{markets}} markets.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical albums, markets, release dates and streams. Real markets can span several time zones; here each market has one zone for releases.
sections.criteria: Local dates in the market's zone; day numbers by date arithmetic; first week as days 0–6 with exact boundaries at local midnight (Hard+); the minimum floor as "at least" (Hard+); robust to a clock change inside the week (Very Hard); correct counts, rounding and order; can discuss late data and pre-aggregation grain.

clarifications.q: Is release day the first 24 hours after release?
clarifications.a: It is the local calendar date of release in the market. On a day the clocks change it is 23 or 25 hours long.

clarifications.q: A stream at exactly local midnight at the start of release day.
clarifications.a: Day 0: it counts in both columns.

clarifications.q: Does the first week end after 168 hours?
clarifications.a: It ends at local midnight at the end of day 6. Compare local dates, not elapsed hours.

clarifications.q: Which time zone applies, the listener's or the market's?
clarifications.a: The market's (markets.tz), for every stream in that market.

clarifications.q: How is the share rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of release_day_streams over first_week_streams, half away from zero.

hints: (stream_ts AT TIME ZONE m.tz)::date is the local date; subtracting two dates in PostgreSQL gives an integer number of days.
Compute the day number once in a CTE, filter to days 0–6, then count with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE day_no = 0).
Never add an interval of hours to a local midnight to find the end of the week: a clock change inside the week moves the boundary by an hour.
followups: Labels want the same share by hour of release day, in local time. What does the hour axis look like in a market whose clocks change that day?
A market spans several time zones. Should release follow each listener's zone or one zone per market, and how would either choice change this report?

The streams table grows by billions of rows a day. How would you partition and pre-aggregate so this report reads days, not raw streams, and what grain must the aggregate keep to stay correct across time zones?
Streams arrive up to three days late from offline devices. When is a first-week number final, and how would you show a number that is still moving?

rules.ask: Which calendar does your date come from? A stream at 00:30 in Tokyo on release day: what UTC date does it have?
What happens to your week boundary when the clocks fall back inside the week?
Your BETWEEN covers which day numbers exactly? Is day 7 inside it?
The release rule is per market. What would per-listener zones change, and which number would a label then compare across markets?
If you pre-aggregate by UTC hour, can you still compute local days for a market at UTC+5:30?

templates.title: Yearly summary: a listener's own top five artists
templates.subtopic: per-partition top-N with ROW_NUMBER, deterministic tie-breaks, filtered aggregates

sections.scenario: Each year a streaming service shows every listener a personal summary of their listening. One card lists the listener's top five artists of the year by minutes listened. Only the listener sees their own summary. The card must be reproducible: computed again from the same plays, it must list the same five artists in the same order.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns listener_id, artist_rank, artist_id, minutes for the year {{year}}, ordered by listener_id, artist_rank. A play counts when ms_played is at least 30 000 (this exercise's rule) and played_at is in {{year}} (UTC). A track's artist is tracks.artist_id. For each listener, rank the artists with counted plays by total counted ms_played descending; equal totals are ordered by the artist's first counted play (earliest played_at first), then by artist_id. Return ranks 1 to 5 (fewer if the listener has fewer artists). minutes is the total counted milliseconds divided by 60 000, rounded to 1 decimal place. {{scope_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Exactly five rows per listener with five or more artists, even when totals tie. A play of exactly 30 000 ms counts. The sample has {{plays}} plays by {{listeners}} listeners.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical listeners, artists and plays; one artist per track. The 30-second rule, the tie-break and the private-session rule are this exercise's rules, not any product's.
sections.criteria: Counted plays filtered before aggregation (30-second rule inclusive, year as a half-open UTC range, private sessions excluded at Hard+); ranking on milliseconds with the first-counted-play tie-break and artist_id last; exactly five rows via ROW_NUMBER; correct rounding and order; can discuss scale, deletions and local years.

clarifications.q: Do short plays count toward anything, such as the first play?
clarifications.a: No. A play under 30 seconds is not a counted play; it neither adds minutes nor decides a tie.

clarifications.q: Two artists tie for fifth place.
clarifications.a: The one the listener played first (first counted play) is fifth; the other is not shown.

clarifications.q: Which year boundaries?
clarifications.a: From {{year}}-01-01 00:00:00 UTC inclusive to {{next_year}}-01-01 00:00:00 UTC exclusive.

clarifications.q: Is ranking on the rounded minutes?
clarifications.a: No. Rank on total milliseconds; round only for display.

clarifications.q: How are minutes rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(total_ms / 60000.0, 1), half away from zero.

hints: Filter to counted plays first, then aggregate per listener and artist: SUM(ms_played) and MIN(played_at).
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY listener_id ORDER BY total_ms DESC, first_play, artist_id); RANK() would let a tie return six rows.
Use a half-open range on played_at for the year rather than EXTRACT(YEAR …) or BETWEEN.
followups: The summary must be computed once for hundreds of millions of listeners and shown on a fixed date. How would you compute top five per listener without one global sort?
A listener deletes some of their history after the summary was computed. What should happen to the card, and how would you support it?
Listeners in Sydney and Honolulu see their year end at different instants. What would change if the year were the listener's local year, and which plays move?
A track credits two artists. How would you split or share minutes, and how would you explain the choice on the card?

rules.ask: Two artists tie for fifth. How many rows does your query return for that listener?
Is a play at exactly midnight on {{next_year}}-01-01 inside your year, and should it be?
Does your first play include plays under 30 seconds, and can a short play decide a tie?
Do you rank on rounded minutes or on milliseconds? Give a case where the two disagree.
LIMIT applies to the whole result. How do you get five rows per listener?

templates.title: Playlist reorder: the fewest track moves
templates.subtopic: longest increasing subsequence by patience sorting, hash maps

sections.scenario: A listener edits a long playlist on one device and the new order must reach their other devices. Rather than resend the whole playlist, the sync sends a small diff: removals, additions and single-track moves ("take this track and put it there"). The fewer moves, the smaller the diff and the less it disturbs anyone listening on another device. You are writing the function that says how small the diff can be.
sections.problem: Implement reorder_moves(old, new). old and new are the playlist's track ids before and after the edit, in playlist order. Return (removed, added, moves): the number of entries in old that are not in new, the number of entries in new that are not in old, and the fewest moves that put the entries kept from old into the order they have in new. A move takes one entry and puts it anywhere else in the list. {{churn_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 entries in each list. A quadratic algorithm is far too slow at that size; aim for O(n log n).
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical playlists and track ids. Real sync protocols also carry versions and conflicts; this exercise counts the diff only.
sections.criteria: Reduces the problem to n − LIS over old positions in new order; O(n log n) with bisect; removals and additions kept out of the moves (Hard+); copies matched in order (Very Hard); correct empty and trivial cases; can explain why the LIS entries stay still and outline recovering the moves.

clarifications.q: Does removing a track count as a move?
clarifications.a: No. Removals and additions are counted separately and are never moves.

clarifications.q: Why is the answer not the number of tracks whose position changed?
clarifications.a: Moving one track shifts every track between its old and new place; those did not move themselves.

clarifications.q: Two empty playlists?
Does it matter where the moves happen?
clarifications.a: No. Only how many are needed.

hints: Map each kept entry to its position in old, then read those positions in new order. The entries you do not move must already be in increasing order.
The fewest moves is the number of kept entries minus the longest increasing subsequence of that position sequence.
Patience sorting: keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1, and place each value with bisect_left.
followups: Return the moves themselves, not just their number: which tracks move, and to where, in an order a client can apply one by one?
Two devices edit the same playlist offline. How would you merge two diffs computed against the same base, and which conflicts can you not resolve automatically?
The sync service sees millions of playlist edits an hour, most touching a few tracks of a long playlist. How would you avoid an O(n log n) pass over the whole playlist for each small edit?

rules.ask: LCS of two lists of n entries is O(n²) in general. What property of these lists lets you do better?
What does list.index cost inside a loop over 200 000 tracks, and what would you use instead?
Is it bisect_left or bisect_right, and what would the other one do here?
One track goes from the end to the top. How many positions changed, and how many moves were needed?
A track appears twice in both lists. How do you decide which copy in old is which copy in new?

templates.title: Album completion: the shortest stretch that plays a whole album
templates.subtopic: two pointers with counts, grouping and stable sorting

sections.scenario: An artist analytics team wants an aggregate measure of how albums are listened to: do listeners take an album in one sitting, or reach every track over weeks of shuffled listening? The building block is, per listener, the shortest stretch of their own consecutive plays that contains every track of the album at least once. The function runs over each listener's plays in a batch job; only aggregates of its output ever reach a report.
sections.problem: Implement shortest_completion(plays, album). album is a list of distinct track ids. {{shape_rule}} {{short_rule}} For each listener, take their plays in order as a sequence and find the shortest run of consecutive plays that contains every album track at least once; plays of other tracks inside the run count toward its length. Return a dict {listener_id: (length, start)} where start is the run's 0-based index in that listener's own sequence; on a tie, the earliest start. Leave out listeners whose plays never contain the whole album.
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 plays, an album of up to 30 tracks. Some album tracks are rare in a listener's history: trying every start position and scanning forward is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical listeners, tracks and plays. Ordering by play start is this exercise's rule; the output is an intermediate result for aggregate reporting, never shown per listener.
sections.criteria: Per-listener sequences; a two-pointer window with counts and a distinct-present counter; strictly-shorter updates giving the earliest start; arrival-order input sorted stably by timestamp (Hard+); short plays removed before indexing (Very Hard); O(n) after grouping with a clear argument; credible discussion of streaming state and many albums.

clarifications.q: Do another listener's plays break a stretch?
clarifications.a: No. Each listener has their own sequence; other listeners' plays are not in it.

clarifications.q: An album of one track?
clarifications.a: The first play of that track: length 1.

clarifications.q: Does an album track played twice inside the run matter?
clarifications.a: It counts toward the run's length like any other play.

clarifications.q: Empty input?
clarifications.a: Return {}.

hints: Group plays per listener first; the problem is then independent per listener.
Expand a right pointer, counting album tracks in the window and how many distinct ones are present; while all are present, record the window and advance the left pointer.
Record only strictly shorter windows: as the right end moves forward, the first window of a given length you find has the earliest start.
followups: Report per album the median completion length across listeners who completed it. What does leaving out non-completers do to that number, and how would you report them?
Plays arrive as a stream, per listener in order. How would you maintain each listener's current shortest stretch incrementally, and how much state per listener and album does that need?
You need this for 50 000 albums at once. Running the window once per album is too slow. How would you restructure the job?

rules.ask: How many steps does your scan take when one album track appears once every few thousand plays?
Building a set per window costs its length. What would you keep instead so each step is O(1)?
Is your sort stable, and do plays with equal timestamps keep their arrival order?
When the left pointer drops an album track whose count falls to zero, what must happen before you can record another window?
How would you express "shortest window containing all tracks" in a dataframe, and what would it cost?

templates.title: Play queue edits: the final order after play next, add to queue, remove, move and skip
templates.subtopic: doubly linked list over a dict, sentinels, O(1) edits

sections.scenario: A listener starts a playlist or an album, and the player builds a queue from it. While it plays, the listener edits the queue: "play next" on one track, "add to queue" on a few more, removing a track they changed their mind about, dragging an entry to a new place, and skipping ahead. The queue the listener sees has two parts: entries the listener queued themselves come first, and the rest of the playlist or album (the context) follows. A long-running session on a smart speaker can collect hundreds of thousands of edits against a very long context, and the client replays the edit log to rebuild the queue after a restart. The rebuild must be fast and give exactly the order the listener saw.
sections.problem:
Implement apply_queue(context, ops). context is the list of entry ids from the playlist or album, in play order. Each entry id is unique and is never reused, even after the entry has played or been removed. Every entry belongs to one of two parts, and the queue always shows the whole queued part followed by the whole context part. Context entries start in the context part. Apply the operations in order (these are this exercise's rules, not a description of any real player):

  1. ('next', e) puts the new entry e at the very front of the queue, in the queued part.
  2. ('add', e) puts the new entry e at the end of the queued part, immediately before the first context-part entry (or at the end of the queue if the context part is empty).
  3. ('remove', e) takes e out of the queue. If e is not in the queue (it already played or was removed), nothing changes.
  4. ('move', e, after) takes e out and puts it immediately after entry after, in after's part. If after is None, e goes to the very front, in the queued part. If e or after is not in the queue, or after == e, nothing changes.
  5. ('advance',) is a skip or the end of a track: the first entry of the queue leaves it and becomes the one now playing. If the queue is empty, nothing is playing any more.

Return (now_playing, queue): the entry now playing (None if nothing has been advanced to, or the last advance found the queue empty) and the list of entry ids in queue order. {{op_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 context entries and 150 000 operations. Every operation must take constant time on average. Searching a Python list with list.index and inserting with list.insert costs O(n) per edit, which is far too slow at this size.
sections.assumptions: Entry ids, queue sizes and the two-part rule are hypothetical and simplified. The same track can appear in the queue twice as two different entries, which is why the operations use entry ids. New entries in next and add never repeat an id seen before. There is no shuffle or repeat in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Exact final order and now-playing entry; "play next" in front, "add to queue" at the end of the queued part; moved entries take the part of the entry they follow, and None means the front of the queued part; ignored operations on entries no longer in the queue and on after == e; advance on an empty queue returns None; O(1) per operation with a dict-based doubly linked list and sentinels; a clear complexity argument; credible answers on two-part display, shuffle and cross-device state.

clarifications.q: If I add three entries with "add to queue", in what order do they play?
clarifications.a: In the order they were added: each one goes after the queued entries already there, just before the context.

clarifications.q: Does "play next" go in front of entries queued earlier?
clarifications.a: Yes. It goes to the very front, so two "play next" entries play in reverse order of the requests.

clarifications.q: Which part does a moved entry belong to?
clarifications.a: The part of the entry it is placed after; an entry moved to the front (after is None) joins the queued part. So a context entry can become queued and a queued entry can join the context.

clarifications.q: What should a remove or move of an entry that already played do?
clarifications.a: Nothing. The entry is no longer in the queue, and the operation is ignored.

clarifications.q: What does now_playing start as?
clarifications.a: None. It changes only on advance, and an advance on an empty queue sets it back to None.

hints: Every operation names an entry, not a position. What structure lets you find an entry, unlink it and insert next to it without shifting anything else?
Store prev and next for each entry in two dicts. Add sentinel nodes so that "the front", "the end of the queued part" and "the end of the queue" are ordinary nodes you can insert after or before.
One sentinel between the two parts does all the work for "add to queue" and for deciding which part a moved entry ends up in. Check that it does.
followups: The client must show "Next in queue" and "Next from: <playlist>" as two headed lists. How do you produce both from your structure, and how would you show the first 50 entries without walking the whole queue?
The listener turns on shuffle for the context part only, and later turns it off. What do you store so that turning shuffle off restores the original order with the edits kept?
The queue must survive the app restarting on another device mid-session. Do you send the edit log, the final order or both, and how do you keep the two devices from diverging if both edit at once?
A very long context (a 10 000-track playlist) is mostly never reached. How would you avoid materialising all of it while still applying moves that name entries far down the list?

rules.ask: Each of those is O(n). With 150 000 entries and 150 000 edits, how many element shifts or comparisons is that in the worst case?
A deque is fast at both ends. Which of the five operations touch the middle of the queue, and what does a deque cost there?
Which sentinels do you have, and how does the one between the two parts decide where "add to queue" and a moved entry go?
How would you renumber when two moves keep inserting between the same pair of entries, and what does the ordering cost to read?
An entry moved after a context entry must join the context. How do your two lists handle a move across the boundary in constant time?

templates.title: Episode highlights: the best set of non-overlapping clips under a score you are given
templates.subtopic: weighted interval scheduling with binary search

sections.scenario: A podcast app can show a short reel of highlights from an episode so that listeners can sample it before they commit to two hours. An upstream step proposes many candidate clips for each episode, with a start, an end and a score from a scoring function you are given (you do not need to know how it works). Candidate clips overlap heavily: the same moment appears in several clips of different lengths. A reel must not play the same second twice, so the chosen clips cannot overlap. The reel should have the highest total score. This step runs for every new episode as it is published.
sections.problem: Implement pick_highlights(clips, min_gap=0). clips is a list of (clip_id, start_s, end_s, score); each clip covers the half-open range [start_s, end_s) of the episode, in seconds, with end_s > start_s. Choose a set of clips in which every two clips, taken in order of start, satisfy later.start_s - earlier.end_s >= min_gap. With min_gap = 0 that means they do not overlap, and a clip ending at second 120 may be followed by one starting at 120. Return (total_score, clip_count) for the set with the highest total score; when several sets tie on the total, return the one with the fewest clips. An empty list returns (0, 0). {{gap_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 80 000 clips per episode, starts up to four hours into the episode and clips up to 20 minutes long, so a single moment can sit inside thousands of clips. Scores are non-negative integers below 1 000. O(n log n) is expected. A DP that looks at every earlier clip for each clip is O(n²), and walking back from each clip to the first compatible one is O(n × overlap), and neither finishes in time.
sections.assumptions: Scores and clip boundaries are hypothetical and come from a scoring function you are given. Clip ids are unique. Clips are given in no particular order. The reel has no length limit in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Correct (total, count) with fewest clips on ties; half-open ranges, so touching clips are compatible when min_gap is 0; min_gap applied at its exact boundary; (0, 0) for no clips; clips scored 0 left out; sort by end plus binary search for the last compatible clip, O(n log n); no recursion that overflows; a clear argument why greedy fails; sensible answers on length limits, reconstruction and batch re-cuts.

clarifications.q: Do two clips that touch, one ending at 120 and the next starting at 120, overlap?
clarifications.a: No, ranges are half-open. With min_gap = 0 both may be chosen. With a positive min_gap they may not.

clarifications.q: Why return the count and not the clip ids?
clarifications.a: Several selections can tie on total and on count. The pair (total, count) with the fewest-clips rule is unique, so it can be checked exactly.

clarifications.q: Can a score be 0?
clarifications.a: Yes. A clip scored 0 never raises the total, and the fewest-clips rule keeps it out.

clarifications.q: Are clips sorted?
clarifications.a: No. Sort them yourself if your approach needs it.

hints: Sort the clips by end time. For clip i, the best selection that ends with clip i uses clip i plus the best selection among clips that end at or before start_i - min_gap.
That set of clips is a prefix of the sorted order. Find where it stops with bisect on the list of end times.
Compare (total, -count) tuples: one max then applies both rules at once.
followups: Producers want the reel to be at most 90 seconds long. What changes in your DP, and what does the extra dimension cost?
Return the chosen clip ids too, with a deterministic rule for ties. Which rule would you pick, and how do you reconstruct the choice from the DP table?

The scoring function changes and every episode in a back catalogue of millions must be re-cut. How would you run this as a batch, and how do you check that the new reels are not worse by some measure you can defend?
Some clips must not be cut mid-sentence: you are also given sentence boundaries. How would you snap clip ends to them before selection, and does that change the algorithm?

rules.ask: Give three clips where your greedy choice loses to another set. What does the greedy rule ignore?
If you sort by start, which earlier clips are compatible with clip i, and are they still a contiguous block you can binary search?
With min_gap greater than 0, what exact value do you search for, and do you use bisect_left or bisect_right? Show the clip that sits exactly on the boundary.
How deep does your recursion go with 80 000 clips, and what does Python do at that depth?
Clip boundaries come from a model as floating-point seconds. Where could comparing them exactly go wrong, and how would you make the boundary rule exact?

templates.title: Debug the artist audience report
templates.subtopic: counting rules, credits, distinct listeners, local-time windows

sections.scenario: Artists see a small report of their audience over the last 28 days: how many streams their music had and how many different listeners played it. Several artists have written in. One says a track they were featured on, a hit, shows no streams for them at all. One says their listener count is higher than the number of people they know listened, and those people listen on a phone, a laptop and a speaker. One, based in Tokyo, says their numbers change in the middle of their morning, not at midnight. One says a whole month of plays disappeared when their label took an old track down. Another noticed that a test listen of exactly half a minute never shows up. The report function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix artist_audience(plays, tracks, artists, as_of) so that it meets this specification. These are this exercise's rules, not a description of how any real service counts streams. {{report_rule}}

  1. Inputs. plays is a list of {"listener", "device", "track", "ts", "ms"}: ts is the play's start in UTC epoch seconds and ms the milliseconds played. tracks maps a track id to {"primary": artist, "featured": [artists], "removed": bool}; every played track is in it, and featured never repeats the primary artist. artists maps every artist named on a track to a fixed UTC offset in minutes (no daylight saving in this exercise). as_of is a date, "YYYY-MM-DD".
  2. Streams. A play counts as a stream when ms is at least 30 000. Shorter plays count for nothing.
  3. Credits. Each stream is credited to the track's primary artist and to every featured artist.
  4. Window. For each artist, only streams that started within the 28 calendar days ending with as_of count, where the calendar day is the artist's own local day (UTC time plus the artist's offset). So the window starts at local midnight 27 days before as_of and ends at local midnight after as_of.
  5. Removed tracks. A track removed from the catalogue since still counts for the plays that happened.
  6. Listeners. The number of distinct listener ids with at least one counted stream for the artist. A listener on several devices is one listener.
  7. Output. {artist: {"streams": n, "listeners": m}} for every artist in artists, including those with zeros.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Up to 200 000 plays, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: All ids, offsets, thresholds and windows are hypothetical. Each play is delivered once. Offsets are whole or half hours between UTC−12 and UTC+12.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with the complaint it causes; 30 000 ms counts; featured artists credited with streams and listeners; listeners distinct across devices; the window taken in each artist's local calendar, at its exact boundaries; removed tracks still counted; zeros reported; the fix stays minimal and linear; adds a regression check per bug.

clarifications.q: Is a play of exactly 30 seconds a stream?
clarifications.a: Yes, 30 000 ms or more counts.

clarifications.q: Whose time zone defines the window when a track has artists in two places?
clarifications.a: Each artist's own. The same play can fall inside the window for one credited artist and outside it for another.

clarifications.q: Does a featured artist also get the listener?
clarifications.a: Yes. Streams and listeners are both credited to every artist on the track.

clarifications.q: Should removed tracks be skipped because they are no longer in the catalogue?
clarifications.a: No. The plays happened, so they count.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Read the 30-second check out loud with the value 30 000.
Make a track with one featured artist, play it once, and read what the report says for that artist.
Take a play at 20:00 UTC on as_of. What is the local date for an artist at UTC+9, and does the code see the same date?
What exactly goes into the listener set?
followups: An artist changes their profile's time zone. Do last month's numbers change, and what should the report say about it?
The report must also be correct for listeners' deletions: a listener who deletes their account. What do you recompute, and how do you avoid exposing that one person left?

Distinct listeners over 28 days across millions of artists is too expensive to recompute from raw plays every day. What would you store per day, and why are daily distinct counts not enough on their own?
A label disputes the featured credit on a track, and it is corrected a week later. How do the past 28 days look before and after, and what does the artist see?

rules.ask: An artist with 40 listeners sees 42. Where would you use an approximate count and where must it be exact?
This exercise uses fixed offsets. What changes for an artist in a region with daylight saving, on the day the clocks change?
Which date does a play at 22:00 UTC belong to for an artist at UTC+9, and for one at UTC−5?
What is the device for in this report, and where would counting per device ever be the right answer?
Which questions should still count plays of a removed track, and which should not?

templates.title: Podcast episode ingestion from hosting feeds
templates.subtopic: feed polling, episode identity, edits, removals, duplicate feeds

sections.scenario: Many podcasts are hosted outside the streaming service: the show's hosting provider publishes an RSS feed, and the show's creator submits that feed once. From then on the service reads the feed and keeps the show's episodes in its catalogue up to date. There are {{shows}} submitted shows across about {{hosts}} hosting providers. Creators expect a new episode to appear within {{freshness}} of being published. Feeds are written by many different systems and are not always tidy: episodes are edited after release, removed, re-published under a new identifier, and the largest feeds hold {{largest_feed}}. Some shows also move to a new host, and for a while two feeds describe the same show.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that keeps the catalogue in step with the feeds. Cover how you schedule fetching so that active feeds are fresh and dormant ones are cheap, how you fetch politely and cheaply (conditional requests, per-host limits), how you parse and validate a feed, how you decide whether an item is a new episode, an edit of a known one or a re-publication, what a removal looks like and what you do about it, how you handle a show that moves to a new feed or is submitted twice, where audio files are fetched and checked, and what you record so that support can explain to a creator why an episode did or did not appear.
sections.constraints: Every change to an episode must be traceable to the feed version that caused it. An episode that disappears from a feed for one fetch because of a host error must not vanish from listeners' libraries. A feed can be very large, and most fetches return nothing new. Hosting providers must never see more requests than an agreed per-host rate.
sections.assumptions: Show counts, freshness targets, feed sizes and host counts are hypothetical. Feeds are RSS with each item carrying a title, a publication date, an audio enclosure URL and usually a unique identifier (a GUID). Some hosts can notify subscribers of updates by a push protocol; most cannot. Specific feed tags that announce a move to a new feed URL exist, but support for them varies by host (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.criteria: A stable catalogue episode id mapped from feed identifiers with a fallback; versioned feed snapshots and diff-based change sets; adaptive per-feed scheduling with conditional requests and per-host limits; a removal rule that tolerates truncated or failed fetches; explicit handling of edits, especially audio replacement; duplicate and moved feeds merged into one show deliberately; audio fetched and validated separately from metadata; an audit trail support can read; a credible plan for each follow-up.

clarifications.q: Can I rely on the GUID being stable?
clarifications.a: Mostly. Some hosts change GUIDs when they migrate, and a few feeds have no GUID at all, so you need a fallback.

clarifications.q: What counts as an edit?
clarifications.a: A changed title, description, artwork, publication date or audio file for the same episode. A changed audio file matters most, because it changes what listeners hear and the episode's duration.

clarifications.q: What should happen when an item disappears from a feed?
clarifications.a: That is your design decision. The creator may have removed it on purpose, or the host may have truncated the feed to its latest items.

clarifications.q: Are listener libraries and play history in scope?
clarifications.a: Only as consumers: they hold episode ids, so episode identity must not change under them.

clarifications.q: How fresh must a dormant show be?
clarifications.a: Dormant shows still need to notice a new episode, but the {{freshness}} target applies to shows that publish regularly.

hints: Separate the catalogue's episode id from the feed's identifier. Map one to the other, so that a GUID change does not create a new episode id for listeners.
Store every fetched feed version (or its normalised item list) with a content hash, and compute the change set by comparing with the previous version. Most fetches then end at "unchanged".
Schedule each feed by how often it actually publishes, and use conditional requests, so that most fetches are cheap and dormant feeds are polled rarely.
followups: A host returns a feed with only the latest 50 items, and next hour returns all {{largest_feed}} again. What does your pipeline do in each fetch?
A show moves to a new host. For two weeks both feeds exist, with different GUIDs for the same episodes. How do you keep one show and one episode id per episode?
A creator replaces an episode's audio with an edited version, ten minutes shorter. What do listeners who were halfway through see, and what do analytics do with plays of the old version?
A host goes down for six hours, then comes back and every one of its feeds changes at once. How do you catch up without breaking the per-host limit or starving other hosts?
Support must answer "why is my episode not showing" within minutes. What do you keep, and what does the support view show?

rules.ask: Two feeds for the same show give different GUIDs for the same episode. What else would you match on, and how sure must you be before merging?
The host served a truncated feed for one fetch. What did your rule just do to the listeners who had those episodes saved?
At {{shows}} shows and a {{freshness}} target, how many fetches an hour is that, and how many of them return nothing new?
Most hosts cannot push. How do push and polling share one scheduler, and what if a push is lost?
A host ignores conditional headers and returns the full feed every time. What does your pipeline do with a full body that has not changed?

templates.title: Collaborative playlist edits from many devices
templates.subtopic: concurrent list edits, operation logs, offline merges, version history

sections.scenario: Any playlist can be made collaborative: the owner invites friends, and every collaborator can add, remove and reorder tracks. There are about {{playlists}} collaborative playlists. A popular one at a party has up to {{collaborators}} people editing it from their phones at the same time, while a desktop app and a speaker show it. Phones can go offline on a plane or in the underground and keep editing for up to {{offline_window}} before they reconnect. Playlists can hold up to {{max_tracks}} tracks. People expect every device to settle on the same playlist, no edit to vanish without a reason, and the owner to be able to see who changed what and to go back to an earlier version.
sections.problem: Design how playlist edits are recorded, ordered, merged and stored. Cover the identity of a playlist item (versus a track), the operations a client sends and what each one refers to, how concurrent edits from several devices are ordered and merged, how an offline device's edits are applied when it reconnects much later, what happens when two edits conflict (a move of an item someone else removed, two people moving the same item, the same track added twice), how the current playlist and its history are stored and read cheaply, how version history and restore work, and what the analytics events for collaboration look like.
sections.constraints: Every device must converge to the same order. A reconnecting device must not overwrite other people's changes with its stale copy. Reading the current playlist must be fast for {{max_tracks}} tracks. History must be kept so that the owner can restore an earlier version, which is itself a new change, not a rewrite of history.
sections.assumptions: Counts, windows and sizes are hypothetical. Each client has a stable device id and the user's account id. The service has a durable store and can order writes for one playlist. You may choose between server-ordered operation logs, revision checks with rebasing, and CRDT-style sequences; say what you give up with each.
sections.criteria: Item ids distinct from track ids; operations that reference items, not positions; a single order of operations per playlist with explicit rebasing or a sequence CRDT, and a stated convergence argument; defined outcomes for remove-versus-move, concurrent moves and duplicate adds, each explainable from history; offline edits applied without overwriting newer changes, and edits from removed collaborators rejected; an operation log with snapshots for fast reads, history and restore-as-a-new-change; analytics events that report collaboration in aggregate; credible answers to the follow-ups.

clarifications.q: Can the same track be in a playlist twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, as two items. Removing one must not remove the other.

clarifications.q: What does a client send for a reorder?
clarifications.a: Your decision. Positions as indexes, or the item ids it should go after, or a sort key.

clarifications.q: Who wins when two people move the same item at once?
clarifications.a: Your decision, but every device must agree and nobody's edit may be lost silently: the loser should be explainable from history.

clarifications.q: Does an offline device know what others changed?
clarifications.a: No. It edits its last copy and sends its operations when it reconnects, possibly {{offline_window}} later.

clarifications.q: Can the owner remove a collaborator?
clarifications.a: Yes. Edits that collaborator made before removal stay; edits they made offline after removal must be rejected.

hints: Give every added item its own id and make every operation refer to item ids, not to index positions. An index is only meaningful in one version of the list.
Order operations per playlist with a revision number. A client sends the revision its edit was based on; the server rebases operations that refer to items, and rejects or transforms the rest.
Store the operation log as the source of truth with periodic snapshots: read = latest snapshot plus the operations since; history and restore = replay to a revision.
followups: A phone reconnects after {{offline_window}} with 40 moves and 3 removes against a playlist that has since changed 2 000 times. Walk through what the server does with each kind of operation.
Two collaborators move the same item at the same moment, to different places. What does each device show a second later, and what does history say?
The owner restores last Tuesday's version. What exactly is written, and what happens to an edit that arrives from an offline phone based on a revision before the restore?
Sort keys between neighbours (fractional indexes) keep growing when people repeatedly insert in the same gap. How do you detect it and rebalance without breaking clients that are mid-edit?
What events would you emit so that product analytics can report collaboration per playlist without storing which person listened to what?

rules.ask: A client sends "move position 4 to position 9" based on revision 30, and the server is at revision 33 with an insert at position 2. What does your server do?
Whose clock decides, and what happens to a phone whose clock is three hours fast?
What does your sequence store per item, how large does that grow for a {{max_tracks}}-track playlist, and how do you compact it?
A collaborator on a plane holds the lock. How does anyone else edit?
How often do you snapshot, and how long does the slowest read take at {{collaborators}} editors making changes every few seconds?

templates.title: Playlist types as data — editorial, personalised, user-made and collaborative, as of a date
templates.subtopic: playlist versions, membership and positions, generated versus edited playlists, as-of queries

sections.scenario: A streaming service holds about {{playlists}} playlists of four kinds. Editorial playlists are curated by the service's editors, can differ by market and are re-ordered often. Personalised playlists are generated for each listener from a scoring function you are given and are regenerated {{personalised_refresh}}; every listener gets their own copy. User-made playlists belong to one listener, who adds, removes and re-orders tracks and episodes and can make the playlist public or private. Collaborative playlists let invited members add, remove and re-order items. Listeners, editors and members together make about {{daily_edits}} playlist edits a day. Analysts want to know how many plays started from a playlist and which version of it was live at the time; support wants to answer "what was in this playlist on that date"; editors want follower counts over time. In this scenario the service keeps playlist history for {{history_years}} years.
sections.problem: Design the data model for playlists across the four kinds. Cover: the playlist entity and what differs by kind (owner, members, market, generator); how items and their positions are stored so that any past version can be reconstructed; what a version is (each edit, each generation run, or something coarser) and how a play is linked to the version that was live when it started; follows and unfollows; visibility changes; and the facts that answer "plays started from each editorial playlist per day and market", "what did this playlist hold on a given date, in order" and "followers per playlist per day". Estimate the storage for history at {{daily_edits}} edits a day and say how you keep it affordable.
sections.constraints: Any playlist's contents and order on a past date must be reconstructable within the {{history_years}}-year history. A personalised playlist is visible only to its listener; analytics on personalised playlists use aggregates across listeners. Plays must be attributable to the playlist they started from without storing a copy of the playlist per play. A deleted account's user-made playlists and their history are removed according to the deletion policy, and their contribution to aggregates is handled explicitly.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates and the history period are hypothetical. The scoring function that fills personalised playlists is given and out of scope; you only store what it produced and when. An item is a track or an episode with a stable id. A playlist can contain the same item more than once.
sections.criteria: Playlist identity separated from versions and edits; an entry id per occurrence so duplicates and moves are representable; a clear definition of a version for each kind (edit, generation run, market variant); validity intervals so plays join to the live version by time; storage estimate with diffs or compaction instead of snapshot-per-edit; follows as events with derived daily counts; personalised playlists private to their listener with aggregates only for analysis; deletion handled explicitly; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a re-order an edit?
clarifications.a: Yes. Order matters to listeners and editors, so a move is an edit even though the set of items did not change.

clarifications.q: Can an editorial playlist differ by market?
clarifications.a: Yes. Treat the market variant as part of the model; editors often share most items across markets.

clarifications.q: How is a personalised playlist versioned?
clarifications.a: Each generation run produces a new version for that listener. A listener can also save a personalised playlist as their own, which creates a user-made copy.

clarifications.q: How does a play know its playlist?
clarifications.a: Each play event carries a context: the playlist id it started from, if any. You decide how to find the version.

clarifications.q: Can the same track appear twice?
clarifications.a: Yes, so an item's identity within a playlist is not just the track id.

hints: Separate the playlist (identity, kind, owner) from its versions (contents at a moment) and from the edits that move between versions.
Positions are fragile under inserts and moves. Consider an entry id per item occurrence, with ordering derived from the edit log or from sortable keys.
For "what was live when the play started", an effective-from / effective-to interval per version lets you join plays by time instead of copying contents.
followups: Sketch the tables for playlists, entries and versions, and show how you reconstruct a 200-item playlist as it was on a date.
A collaborative playlist gets two re-orders from two members within the same second. How do your versions and positions stay consistent, and which order does the history show?
Personalised playlists are regenerated {{personalised_refresh}} for every listener. Do you store a full snapshot per generation, a diff, or only the item list with a run id? Estimate the rows.
An analyst asks for plays per editorial playlist per day, split by the version that was live. Write the join, and say what happens to plays that started a few seconds after a re-order.
A listener deletes their account. Which rows go, which aggregates keep their contribution, and how does a collaborative playlist they edited change?

rules.ask: At {{daily_edits}} edits a day, how many item rows does a full snapshot per edit write, and what would you store instead for a one-item move?
A member moves the last item to the top of a 300-item playlist. How many rows change in your model, and how do you show that move in the history?
What exactly carries the validity interval: the playlist, each entry, or each version? How does a play join to it?
The generator is re-run because of a bug and produces a different list for the same week. Which version did the listener see, and where is that recorded?
Is the follower number a counter on the playlist row or derived from follow events? How do you show followers per day for last year?

incidents: After a generation bug, one run of personalised playlists ({{personalised_refresh}}) was redone in place; the original run's rows were overwritten, and play attribution for those hours now credits items the listeners never saw.
An editor re-orders a large editorial playlist many times in an hour; the snapshot-per-edit table grew far faster than the {{daily_edits}}-a-day estimate, and the nightly compaction fell behind.
A collaborative playlist's history shows an item removed before it was added: two members' edits from different devices carried client timestamps, and one device's clock was minutes behind.

templates.title: Audiobooks and podcasts in one catalogue — series, editions, chapters and included hours
templates.subtopic: spoken-word catalogue, works versus editions, chapters and episodes, plan allowance versus ownership

sections.scenario: A streaming service offers podcasts (about {{shows}} shows, each with episodes, seasons and trailers) and audiobooks (about {{audiobooks}} titles from publishers) in {{markets}} markets. An audiobook can exist in several editions: abridged and unabridged, different narrators, different languages and publishers, each with its own chapters and runtime, and some books belong to a series. Rights differ by market and change over time. In this scenario some plans include {{included_hours}} hours of audiobook listening a month (this exercise's rule; check current docs), and a listener can also buy an audiobook, which they then keep. Listeners resume where they left off on any device. Product teams want listening hours by title, edition and series; finance wants included hours used per plan and month; listeners see their own remaining hours.
sections.problem: Design the data model for one spoken-word catalogue holding podcasts and audiobooks. Cover: shows, seasons and episodes; works, editions, series and the order within a series; contributors (authors, narrators, hosts) as roles; chapters with offsets; market availability over time; listening progress per listener and edition; and the allowance model: how included hours are measured, consumed, reset each month and reconciled with purchases. Say which facts answer "hours listened per edition, per market and day", "share of included hours used per plan and month" and "titles started under the allowance and later purchased".
sections.constraints: A listener's remaining included hours shown to them must never be less accurate than what they are charged against. A purchase is permanent for that listener even if the title later leaves the plan or the market. Progress must survive a publisher re-delivering an edition with different chapter boundaries. Podcast and audiobook analytics share dimensions (date, market, contributor) but never mix a podcast episode with an audiobook chapter in the same measure without saying so.
sections.assumptions: Catalogue sizes, markets and the allowance are hypothetical. In this exercise the allowance counts time actually listened, so an hour of audio at double speed uses thirty minutes; check current docs for any real plan's rule. Offline listening is reported when the device reconnects. The allowance resets on the plan's monthly billing date in the listener's time zone.
sections.criteria: Works separated from editions, with series order and contributor roles; podcasts and audiobooks as distinct item kinds sharing dimensions; progress as an offset within an edition, chapters as ranges; market availability with validity intervals; the allowance as a ledger with usage, resets and top-ups, measured in listening time and attributed by when listening happened; purchases as permanent entitlements independent of plan availability; facts at stated grains; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is an edition a separate title?
clarifications.a: It is a separate product with its own runtime, chapters and rights, but it belongs to one work. Reports need both levels.

clarifications.q: Does re-listening use allowance?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise every minute listened under the allowance counts, including re-listening.

clarifications.q: What happens when the allowance runs out mid-book?
clarifications.a: Listening stops until the next reset or a top-up; a listener can buy the book and continue from the same position.

clarifications.q: Can a podcast episode also be an audiobook chapter?
clarifications.a: No. They are separate kinds of items; a show can, however, promote a book.

clarifications.q: Do purchased titles use allowance?
clarifications.a: No. Once purchased, listening to that edition never uses allowance.

hints: Separate the abstract work from its editions; contributors attach to either with a role.
Model progress as position within an edition (an offset in its audio), and chapters as ranges over that offset, so chapters can change without moving the listener.
The allowance is a small ledger per listener and period: usage lines from listening, resets, top-ups, and an entitlement record per purchase.
followups: Draw works, editions, series and contributors. How do you answer "hours listened to this book across all its editions"?
A publisher re-delivers an edition with chapters re-split. What happens to listeners' progress and to "hours per chapter" reports already published?
A listener listens offline for several days, then reconnects after the reset date. Which period's allowance do those minutes use, and what did the listener see meanwhile?
A title leaves the plan in one of the {{markets}} markets while a listener is halfway through it under the allowance. Model what they can do next, and how the analytics show it.
Finance asks for included hours used per plan and month at {{included_hours}} hours included. How do you prove the per-listener ledgers sum to the reported total?

rules.ask: The same book has an abridged and an unabridged edition with different narrators. Where does each live, and how does "hours for this book" work?
The publisher re-splits the chapters. Your progress points to a chapter id that no longer exists. How does the listener resume in the right place?
Two devices report listening for the same listener at once, one of them offline. How does your counter stay correct, and how do you explain the balance to the listener?
The listener bought the book after using plan hours on it. Which minutes count against the allowance, and does the purchase change any past numbers?
Your allowance counts time listened. Which measure do the "hours listened per edition" reports use, and how do you stop the two being confused?

incidents: Offline listening uploaded after the monthly reset was charged to the new period; listeners on the {{included_hours}}-hour allowance saw their new month start partly used and complained.
A publisher re-delivered a popular edition with new chapter boundaries and a re-encoded file a few seconds longer; resume positions now start mid-sentence for listeners in {{markets}} markets.
A rights change removed a title from the plan in some markets overnight; listeners who had already purchased it saw "unavailable" because purchase entitlements were checked against plan availability.

templates.title: Artists, credits and follows — primary and featured artists, claimed profiles and the numbers an artist sees
templates.subtopic: artist profiles and credit roles, profile merges and splits, follow events, artist-facing aggregates

sections.scenario: A streaming service has about {{artists}} artist profiles. A track lists one or more primary artists and, on about {{featured_share}} of tracks, featured artists; credits also name songwriters and producers. Artists or their teams can claim a profile and then see analytics for it. Listeners follow and unfollow artists, about {{daily_follows}} follow changes a day. Some profiles turn out to be duplicates of one artist and are merged; some profiles mix two different artists with the same name and must be split. Artists see daily numbers on their profile and in their analytics: streams, listeners, followers and saves, with breakdowns by country and city shown only when at least {{min_listeners}} listeners are behind a cell (this exercise's rule).
sections.problem: Design the data model for artists, credits and follows, and the aggregates an artist sees. Cover: artist profiles and their lifecycle (created, claimed, merged, split); the credits on each track with roles and order; how a stream is credited to artists (in this exercise every primary and featured artist on a track is credited with the stream, and a listener is counted once per artist per day); follow and unfollow events and the follower number; claims and team access; and the daily aggregates per artist with the minimum-listener rule. Explain how merges and splits change past numbers, and what an artist sees after one.
sections.constraints: An artist sees only aggregates, never individual listeners. Breakdown cells with fewer than {{min_listeners}} listeners are suppressed, and a suppressed cell cannot be recovered by subtracting other published numbers. The follower count on the profile and in analytics must agree after the daily refresh. Credit changes from rights holders are applied from a stated date and leave an audit trail.
sections.assumptions: Counts, shares and the threshold are hypothetical. The stream-counting rule (what counts as a stream) is this exercise's rule and is given upstream; this question starts from counted streams. Songwriter and producer credits are displayed but do not receive stream credit in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Stable profile identity with merge and split events mapping ids; credits as a versioned bridge with roles and order; streams credited per the stated rule with distinct listeners computed per grain, never summed; follows as events with a derived, reconcilable count; claims and team roles controlling access; suppression with complementary-cell protection and consistent refresh; restatement policy for merges, splits and credit changes; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a featured artist's listener count include listeners of the track?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise. A listener who streams a track with a featured artist is a listener of both artists that day.

clarifications.q: What happens to follows when two profiles are merged?
clarifications.a: The merged profile keeps the union of followers; a listener who followed both counts once.

clarifications.q: How does a split decide which follows go where?
clarifications.a: It often cannot. Say what you would do and what the artist sees.

clarifications.q: Who can see a profile's analytics?
clarifications.a: Members of the profile's team after the claim is verified, with roles you define.

clarifications.q: Are follower numbers real-time?
clarifications.a: The profile can show a rounded live number; analytics refresh daily. They must agree after the refresh.

hints: Keep the profile identity stable and record merges and splits as events that map old ids to new ones, rather than rewriting history in place.
Credits are a bridge between tracks and artists with a role and an order, versioned by effective date.
Daily facts per artist are additive for streams but not for listeners; distinct listeners need their own computation at each grain you publish.
followups: Draw artists, credits and follows. How does one stream of a track with two primary artists and one featured artist appear in each artist's daily facts?
Two duplicate profiles are merged. Show the follower count before and after, and what each artist's past daily numbers show.
A profile mixed two artists with the same name for a year. How do you split streams, follows and saves, and what do you tell each artist?
Prove that the city breakdown with the {{min_listeners}}-listener threshold cannot be undone by subtracting the country total and the other cities.
A label re-delivers credits for a back catalogue, moving some featured artists to primary. Which numbers change, from which date, and how is that visible?

rules.ask: A track has two primary artists and a featured artist. How does your track row express that, and how does each of them get credit for a stream?
Follow and unfollow events for one listener arrive out of order after a retry. What does your counter show, and how does the daily refresh fix it?
After a merge, an artist asks why last year's monthly listeners changed. Do you restate history or only change numbers from the merge date, and why?
Can you add a primary artist's listeners and a featured artist's listeners to get the listeners of the track? What do you store to answer distinct counts correctly?
A cell has 49 listeners and the country total is published. How does a reader reconstruct it, and what does your suppression do about it?

incidents: Two artists with the same name were merged by mistake; for a week one artist's profile showed the other's releases, and with about {{daily_follows}} follow changes a day, thousands of new follows went to the wrong artist before the split.
A credits re-delivery moved featured artists to primary on {{featured_share}} of a label's catalogue and was applied to all history; artists whose past numbers dropped opened support tickets.
The country total and the city breakdown were refreshed at different times, and for a small city the difference revealed a suppressed cell below {{min_listeners}} listeners.

templates.title: Playback across devices — handoffs, remote control, offline plays and private sessions
templates.subtopic: device registry, playback state and segments, controller versus player, offline upload, private-session flags

device_mix: phone, TV, games console and smart speaker

sections.scenario: About {{daily_listeners}} listeners a day play music, podcasts and audiobooks on several devices: in this scenario mostly {{device_mix}}. In this exercise one device plays for an account at a time: starting playback on a second device moves it there, and a phone can act as a remote control for a speaker while the speaker plays. Downloaded items play offline and their plays are reported when the device reconnects; in this exercise a device must reconnect at least every {{offline_days}} days to keep downloads. A listener can start a private session, whose plays are not shown in social features and not used as personalisation inputs, but still count as plays under this exercise's counting rule. Devices send about {{events_per_day}} playback events a day (start, progress, pause, seek, skip, transfer, remote command). Analysts want minutes by device type, handoffs between device types, and offline listening; artists receive play counts; each listener sees their own listening history.
sections.problem: Design the data model from raw playback events to analytical facts. Cover: the device registry (type, app version, owner account, a device used by several accounts); the raw event schema with ids and the clocks it carries; how events become playback segments (continuous playback of one item on one device) and how a handoff and a remote-control command are represented; which device is the player and which the controller; offline plays uploaded later; the private-session flag and where it must travel; and the facts that answer "minutes per device type and day", "handoffs between device types per month" and "share of listening that was offline".
sections.constraints: A play is counted once, on the device that played it, never on the controller. Private-session plays never reach social features or personalisation inputs, and the flag survives a handoff. Offline plays are attributed to when they happened, not to when they were uploaded, and a closed reporting period changes only by a documented restatement. A listener's own history may show their own detail; every other consumer sees aggregates.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the device mix and the offline window are hypothetical. Devices carry clocks that can be wrong by minutes; the server records a receive time. Each event has a client-generated event id and a per-device sequence number.
sections.criteria: Raw events, segments and facts as distinct layers; device registry with shared devices; player versus controller made explicit with plays counted only on the player; ordering by device sequence with client, receive and event times kept apart; dedupe by event id and by device sequence; private flag carried on the session and enforced at the consumer boundary; offline plays attributed by occurrence with a restatement policy; aggregates for everyone but the listener; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: What is a handoff?
clarifications.a: Playback of the same item continuing on another device within a few seconds near the same position. You define the window and tolerance.

clarifications.q: Does the controller phone send play events?
clarifications.a: It sends remote commands. The speaker sends the play events. Both carry the account and the session.

clarifications.q: Can two people use the same speaker?
clarifications.a: Yes. The account playing is on each event; the device is shared.

clarifications.q: How late can offline plays arrive?
clarifications.a: Up to {{offline_days}} days in this exercise, and occasionally later from devices that were lost and found.

clarifications.q: Does a private session end on its own?
clarifications.a: In this exercise it ends after a period of inactivity or when the listener turns it off. Model the boundary explicitly.

hints: Keep three layers: raw events as received, cleaned segments (one item, one device, continuous), and facts.
Order events by device and sequence number, not by device clock; record client time, server receive time and your chosen event time separately.
Make the playback session (one account's continuous listening across devices) an entity that carries the private flag, so a handoff inherits it.
followups: Show the rows that one evening produces: start on a phone, transfer to a speaker controlled from the phone, pause, and finish in a car.
Where is the private-session flag stored, and how do you prove it never reaches the personalisation inputs?
Offline plays from the last {{offline_days}} days arrive after the month closed. Which facts change, and what does the monthly report say?
A device's clock is ten minutes fast. Which of your measures are wrong, and how does sequence number plus receive time repair them?
At {{events_per_day}} events a day, how do you build segments incrementally when progress events for one segment span midnight and arrive out of order?

rules.ask: The device clock is wrong by minutes. Which ordering and which day does your segment use, and how do you detect the skew?
Both the phone and the speaker send events while the phone controls playback. Which one counts the play, and what stops it being counted twice?
The listener transfers playback from a phone in a private session to a speaker. How does the speaker's play know it is private?
Offline plays arrive {{offline_days}} days late, after last month was reported. Do you restate the month, add them to the current month, or both? Who sees which number?
A device resends a batch after a timeout with new event ids but the same sequence numbers. How does your dedupe hold up?

incidents: After an app release, phones acting as remote controls began sending their own play events, and minutes on smart speakers were counted twice for listeners on the {{device_mix}} mix until the release was rolled back.
A batch of devices reconnected after {{offline_days}} days offline and uploaded weeks of plays; last month's closed minutes per device type rose and the published report no longer matched.
The private-session flag was set only on the device where the session started; after a handoff to a speaker, private plays reached the personalisation inputs for a day.

templates.title: Device handoffs — playback that continued on another device near the same position
templates.subtopic: next row per listener (LEAD), interval and tolerance boundaries, month attribution, private-session exclusion

sections.scenario: A streaming service records playback as segments: a segment is continuous playback of one item (a track trk_… or an episode ep_…) on one device, with the item position where it started and where it stopped. In this exercise one device plays for a listener at a time, so a listener's segments never overlap. A listener who moves from their phone to a speaker, or from a car to a desktop, produces a segment that ends on one device and a segment that starts on another a few seconds later, near the same position. The product team wants to know how often playback moves between device types, month by month. The sample covers {{months}}: {{listeners}} listeners, {{devices}} devices and {{segments}} segments, all hypothetical.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, from_device_type, to_device_type, handoffs, listeners, one row per combination with at least one handoff, ordered by month, from_device_type, to_device_type. For each segment A, take the same listener's next segment B, in order of started_at and then segment_id. The pair is a handoff when all of these hold (this exercise's rule):

  • B is on a different device_id than A (two phones are two devices; that pair is reported as phone, phone);
  • B plays the same item_id as A;
  • B starts no earlier than A ended and at most 10 seconds after it: A.ended_at <= B.started_at <= A.ended_at + 10 seconds;
  • B's start_position_ms is within {{tol_s}} seconds ({{tol_ms}} ms) of A's end_position_ms, in either direction, inclusive;
  • neither A nor B has private_session true. A private segment is still a segment: it can be another segment's next one.

month is the UTC month of B's started_at as text YYYY-MM. from_device_type and to_device_type are the types of A's and B's devices. handoffs counts the pairs, and listeners counts the distinct listeners with at least one of them in that row.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every boundary is inclusive: exactly 10 seconds, and exactly {{tol_ms}} ms apart, still count. Only the listener's next segment can be B, never a later one. Production holds billions of segments a month.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, listeners, devices and items. Timestamps are stored to the second, positions in milliseconds. A device belongs to whoever is playing on it; devices holds only its type.
sections.criteria: The next segment per listener (LEAD with a deterministic tie-break) rather than any later one; all five conditions with inclusive boundaries and an absolute position difference; device id compared, device type reported; month from B's start in UTC; private segments excluded from both sides but kept when finding the next one; distinct listeners per row; deterministic ordering; can discuss clock skew, units contracts and incremental computation across month boundaries.

clarifications.q: What if the listener resumes on the same device after a pause?
clarifications.a: Not a handoff: the device_id is the same.

clarifications.q: Two speakers of the same type?
clarifications.a: A handoff if they are different device_ids; it is reported as speaker → speaker.

clarifications.q: Which month does a handoff at midnight belong to?
clarifications.a: The month in which B started, in UTC.

clarifications.q: The next segment is a different track on another device, at a similar position?
clarifications.a: Not a handoff: the item must be the same.

clarifications.q: Should I drop private segments before finding the next segment?
clarifications.a: No. They still happened; they are only excluded from being either side of a reported handoff.

hints: LEAD(...) OVER (PARTITION BY listener_id ORDER BY started_at, segment_id) gives each segment's next one without a self-join over all later segments.
Join devices for both sides after you have the pairs, so each side gets its own type.
b.started_at <= a.ended_at + INTERVAL '10 seconds' and ABS(b.start_position_ms - a.end_position_ms) <= {{tol_ms}} keep both boundaries inclusive.
followups: Extend the result with the median gap in seconds per row. Which function do you use, and what does it cost at production volume?
Product wants handoffs as a share: handoffs ÷ segments that ended on the from-device type. Write the denominator so a device type with no handoffs still appears.
A listener switches devices mid-track but the new device starts the next track because of a queue sync delay. Would you widen the rule to the next item in the queue? What breaks?
At billions of segments a month, how do you compute this incrementally, given that a handoff can span midnight and a month boundary?

rules.ask: Your join matches every later segment within 10 seconds. A listener resumed briefly on the same device and then moved. How many handoffs does your query count for that move?
The listener moved from one phone to another phone. Is that a handoff under the rule, and does your condition keep it?
Did you remove private segments before or after finding each segment's next one? Walk through public → private → public on three devices.
Which segment's time decides the month: the one that ended or the one that started? Check a handoff a few seconds either side of midnight on the first of a month.
Good. What does your tolerance do at exactly {{tol_ms}} ms, and why does the direction of the difference not matter?
